newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour to step up battle for business votes.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour to step up battle for business votes.

text.p: The efforts of Britain's opposition Labour party to win the hearts and minds of business chiefs are set to be rewarded this week when a new report on the future of industry backs some of the party's key economic policies.

The report, written by the Commission on Public Policy and British Business, will back Labour's minimum wage policy and criticise the government's antipathy towards a European single currency and the European Union's social chapter.
The Commission was set up by the left-leaning Institute of Public Policy Research and is due to be presented at a conference on Tuesday.

A pro-Labour report from a leftish think-tank could easily slip past senior business leaders unnoticed. But the decision of Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine to address the conference and share a platform with Labour leader Tony Blair means the report is set to get plenty of attention.

The Times newspaper said on Monday that Heseltine, a fearsome free marketeer, all but forced himself onto the conference programme after he became aware the Commission was to support measures that conflict with government policy.
Blair has secured the slot before morning coffee, with Heseltine due to speak just after the break.

Labour, traditionally the ally of trade unions and the low paid, has made strenuous efforts to shed its old tax-and-spend image and present a more business-friendly face. The party is far ahead of the government in opinion polls.

It has hosted a series of business conferences and, according to newspaper reports, Blair has taken advice from a range of senior businessmen including British Airways chief executive Robert Ayling and media group Pearson's chairman-designate Dennis Stevenson.

And the decision by Britain's opposition Labour party on Monday to rule out tax increases in the next Parliament will also help cement the party's rapidly improving relationship with the business community.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown said Labour would not sanction increases in public sector pay or in personal taxation, enhancing his credentials as a tough Chancellor of the Exchequer-in waiting.
Brown will spell out his income tax policies in more detail at a conference later on Monday.

Labour's attempts to woo business appear to be paying off. The latest poll of managers' political allegience conducted by the Institute of Management found that in November only 42 percent of managers backed the Conservatives compared with 62 percent at the last election in 1992.
Support for the Labour Party among the same group has risen to 25 percent from 12 percent in 1992.
But while Labour has made some inroads in winning over business leaders, many managers still find some policies difficult to stomach.
Lobby groups have singled out two key policies for particular criticism -- the minimum wage, and plans for a one-off "windfall" tax on the profits of recently privatised utilities.
On Sunday, one newspaper said Labour planned to raise up to 10 billion pounds ($16.6 billion) from the tax, double the original estimate.
A spokesman for Gordon Brown said on Monday the party would give details of windfall tax plans only if it came to power after the election, which must be held before May this year.
